actions.justification: Mandatory first step for a COPD patient with worsening dyspnea. Assessing respiratory status (work of breathing, accessory muscle use, breath sounds, wheeze) is critical to characterize the severity of the exacerbation.
Mandatory baseline vital sign assessment to establish hemodynamic stability and guide clinical decision-making in AECOPD.
Mandatory chest X-ray to identify potential triggers or complications of COPD exacerbation (e.g., pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema) per AECOPD guidelines.

MANDATORY: ABG is essential in AECOPD to assess PaO2, PaCO2, and pH, which determine severity (hypercapnic respiratory failure) and guide decisions on NIV or mechanical ventilation. Must be completed within 60 minutes.
Mental status assessment is critical in AECOPD to detect CO2 narcosis or encephalopathy, which affects NIV eligibility and urgency of intervention.

Per COPD exacerbation guidelines, NIV eligibility should be assessed early in patients with suspected or confirmed hypercapnic respiratory failure to prepare for possible non-invasive ventilation if ABG confirms respiratory acidosis.
Short-acting bronchodilators (e.g., salbutamol/ipratropium) are first-line treatment for acute COPD exacerbation to relieve bronchospasm and improve airflow.
Systemic corticosteroids (e.g., prednisolone 40mg) are recommended in AECOPD per GOLD guidelines to reduce inflammation, shorten recovery time, and decrease treatment failure risk.

Increased sputum production suggests an infectious (bacterial) trigger for this COPD exacerbation. Antibiotics are indicated per GOLD guidelines when sputum purulence is present or two of three cardinal symptoms (dyspnea, sputum volume, purulence) are present.
CBC to evaluate for leukocytosis suggesting infection/exacerbation severity, anemia contributing to dyspnea, or polycythemia in severe COPD patient.
BMP to assess electrolytes, renal function, and bicarbonate (chronic CO2 retention compensation) in this COPD exacerbation patient.
Severe COPD exacerbation warrants pulmonology consultation for specialist guidance on NIV settings, escalation planning, and management optimization.

Patient with severe COPD exacerbation presenting with increased sputum production. Sputum culture will help identify causative organisms and guide antibiotic therapy, especially important given antibiotics have already been initiated.
Procalcitonin helps differentiate bacterial from viral etiology in COPD exacerbations and can guide antibiotic stewardship decisions.

CT chest provides detailed evaluation of lung parenchyma in this severe COPD patient with worsening dyspnea to rule out pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, or other complications not fully visible on plain chest X-ray.

Controlled supplemental oxygen is indicated for COPD exacerbation to maintain SpO2 88-92% (avoiding hypercapnic drive suppression). Standard supportive care not yet administered per available actions.

Bacterial infection is a common trigger for COPD exacerbation; blood cultures should be obtained to identify causative organism, especially since antibiotics were already started (ideally cultures before antibiotics, but still valuable for sensitivities).
Lactate measurement helps assess for tissue hypoperfusion or sepsis as a complication of the infectious COPD exacerbation, aiding risk stratification.

Patient with severe COPD presenting with dyspnea - while primary workup is underway, a diuretic may help if there is a fluid overload component contributing to dyspnea. With stable vitals (BP 120/80, SpO2 98%), this is a reasonable optional intervention to address potential fluid retention component.

Patient with severe COPD exacerbation may have reduced oral intake and increased insensible losses; cautious IV fluid administration supports hydration while monitoring for fluid overload. No mandatory actions remain and this is the most clinically appropriate available option.
Only available action remaining in this phase. Patient is hemodynamically stable; this action is selected as it is the sole option available, though clinical need is low given current stable vitals.
ABG, CBC, BMP, procalcitonin, sputum culture, and lactate were ordered; reviewing results as they return will guide further management decisions including antibiotic adjustment and NIV escalation.

Multiple labs are marked as pending (CBC, BMP, ABG, procalcitonin, lactate). Reviewing results when available guides further management decisions including antibiotic selection and need for escalation.
Continuous monitoring of SpO2 is essential in COPD exacerbation to ensure adequate but not excessive oxygenation (target 88-92% in COPD to avoid hypercapnic drive suppression).
